01.note: A divorced woman who did not want to go on nursing her baby came before Shmuel. He sent Rav Dimi bar Yosef to test whether the baby knew her. Rav Dimi seated her in a row of women and carried the baby past them. When the baby reached her he looked at her face with joy, and she turned her eyes away. Rav Dimi told her: Lift up your eyes, get up and take your son. The Gemara then asks how a blind baby could know his mother, and Rav Ashi answers: by smell and by the taste of her milk.
01.why: The Gemara has ruled that a divorced mother can be made to keep nursing a baby who already recognizes her, and is asking at what age that happens. Shmuel held there is no fixed age, so each baby must be checked; this case shows such a check.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage the divorced woman comes to; he sends someone to test the baby.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: Sent by Shmuel to check whether the baby recognizes its mother.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Explains how a blind baby would recognize his mother.

02.note: Abaye's tenant farmer asked him whether he could betroth a nursing woman fifteen months after her baby's birth. Abaye said yes, piling up reasons: the law follows Rabbi Yehuda over Rabbi Meir, and Beit Hillel over Beit Shammai; Ulla ruled with Rabbi Yehuda; and Mar Ukva said Rabbi Hanina had let him marry after fifteen months, so a mere betrothal was surely allowed. When Abaye told his teacher Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef answered that Rav and Shmuel both say she must wait twenty-four months. Abaye ran three parasangs after the farmer, and some say one parasang through sand, but he could not catch up with him.
02.why: The Gemara is discussing how long a nursing widow must wait before remarrying: twenty-four months or eighteen, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel shortening each by three. Afterward Abaye draws the lesson that a student should not rule on even a simple matter near his teacher.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Gives his tenant farmer a lenient ruling, then learns from his teacher that it was wrong.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who cites Rav and Shmuel requiring a twenty-four-month wait.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: Rules that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Says Rabbi Hanina allowed him to marry a nursing woman after fifteen months.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which makes the couple legally bound to each other; the wedding and living together come later.
A Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.
The two great early schools of Sages; when they disagree, the law generally follows Beit Hillel.

03.note: Two pious men, who some say were Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas, the sons of Rav Hisda, both fed the waiter who served at their meals. One gave him food before the meal; the other gave it to him after the guests had eaten. Elijah used to speak with the one who fed the waiter first, and did not speak with the other.
03.why: The Gemara has ruled that a waiter should be given a share of foods with a strong aroma or taste, so he does not suffer watching others eat. Like the story of Avuh and Minyamin bar Ihi just before it, this one shows that even timing counts.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: One of two pious men, by one account sons of Rav Hisda.

people.name: Rav Pinehas
people.about: The other of the two pious men, by one account a son of Rav Hisda.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who speaks only with the brother who feeds the waiter first.

terms.meaning: The biblical prophet, who in Talmudic stories still appears to and speaks with especially worthy people.

04.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting at the entrance to the house of King Izgur when the king's chief butler passed by carrying food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra's face go pale with craving, took some food with his finger and put it in his mouth. The butler said he had spoiled the king's meal. Asked why he did it, Rav Ashi said whoever made the dish had spoiled it, because he saw a leprous infection in the meat. They checked and found nothing; he put his finger on one spot, they checked there and found it. When the Sages asked why he had relied on a miracle, he said he had seen a spirit of leprosy hovering over the food.
04.why: The Gemara has ruled that someone who smells or sees a tempting food should be given some, since the craving can endanger him; this is one of several incidents showing that rule in action.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Feeds Mar Zutra from the king's food and defends himself by finding a defect in it.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Goes pale with craving at the sight of the king's food.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Sits with the other two Sages at the king's gate.

people.name: King Izgur
people.about: The king at whose house the Sages are sitting.

terms.meaning: The biblical skin disease often called leprosy; here the word is used for a defect in the meat that made it unfit for the king.

05.note: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He brought pomegranates, peeled them and ate them in front of her without offering her any. She swallowed the saliva that tormented her until she became ill. At last he asked: If I cure you, will you marry me? She said yes. He brought pomegranates again, peeled and ate them in front of her, and told her to spit out all the saliva that troubled her. She did, until something like a green leaf came out of her, and she was cured.
05.why: The Gemara has ruled that anyone present when a food with a strong aroma or taste is served should be given some; this story, after the one about Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra, shows how much harm an unsatisfied craving can do.

06.note: A Jew and a gentile were walking along a road together, and the gentile could not keep up. He reminded the Jew of the destruction of the Temple. The Jew sighed and groaned, but the gentile still could not keep up. The gentile said: Don't you people say that groaning breaks half a person's body? The Jew answered that this holds only for a new sorrow, not for one they are used to, as people say: a woman used to losing her children does not panic.
06.why: Rav and Rabbi Yohanan have just disagreed over how much of the body groaning breaks, and the Gemara has said the news of the Temple's destruction is especially crushing. The Jew's answer qualifies that: a long-familiar grief no longer breaks the body.

terms.meaning: The central sanctuary of the Jewish people in Jerusalem; its destruction was mourned as the great national catastrophe.

07.note: Rabbi Abbahu was standing in a bathhouse, held up by two slaves, when the bathhouse collapsed under him. He found a pillar, climbed out and pulled both of them up. Rabbi Yohanan was going up stairs, held up by Rav Ami and Rav Asi, when the stair collapsed under him; he climbed up and pulled them both up. The Sages asked him why, if he was that strong, he needed people to support him. He answered: If so, what will I leave for my old age?
07.why: The Gemara is defining the 'men of leisure' who, by the mishna, owe their wives marital relations every day. Ravin has just said these are the pampered men of the Land of Israel, and these two incidents are told to show how strong they were.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Climbs out of a collapsing bathhouse and pulls up the two slaves who were supporting him.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Saves himself and his two helpers when a stair gives way, then explains why he still lets them support him.

people.name: Rav Ami
people.about: One of the two who were supporting Rabbi Yohanan on the stairs.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The other of the two supporting Rabbi Yohanan on the stairs.

08.note: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava in Mehoza and used to come home once a year, on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he was caught up in his study and did not go. His wife waited for him, saying: Now he is coming, now he is coming. He did not come. She was distressed and a tear fell from her eye. At that moment he was sitting on a roof; the roof collapsed under him and he died.
08.why: Rav Adda bar Ahava has reported, in Rav's name, that the Rabbis let students leave home for two or three years of Torah study without their wives' permission. Rava says Sages acted on this and it sometimes ended in death; this story is his example.

people.name: Rav Rehumi
people.about: A student of Rava who came home once a year; he dies the year he fails to come.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage in Mehoza with whom Rav Rehumi studied.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year, a day of fasting and prayer.

09.note: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya and son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai, spent his time in the study hall and came home every Friday at dusk. Whenever he came, Rabbi Yannai would see a pillar of fire going before him. One week he was caught up in his study and did not come. When Rabbi Yannai did not see the sign, he told the family: Turn his bed over, for if Yehuda were alive he would not have missed his time with his wife. His words were like 'an error that proceeds from a ruler', and Yehuda died.
09.why: Shmuel has just said that the proper time for Torah scholars to be with their wives is Friday night; Yehuda keeps exactly that schedule, and the story follows Rav Rehumi's as another death tied to a scholar who failed to come home.

people.name: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Rabbi Yannai's son-in-law, who studies all week and comes home every Friday at dusk.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: Yehuda's father-in-law, who sees a pillar of fire before him and, when it is missing, declares him dead.

terms.meaning: Overturning the beds of the house was a mourning custom; saying it meant treating Yehuda as already dead.

terms.term: an error that proceeds from a ruler
terms.meaning: A phrase from Ecclesiastes 10:5, used here for a great man's mistaken words, which came true anyway.

10.note: Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the girl died when they came to write the marriage contract. Looking into the families, they found Rabbi descended from King David's wife Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother Shimi. Rabbi then matched his son with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, with twelve years of study planned before the wedding. When the girl was brought past him, the son cut it to six years; brought past again, he said he would marry first and study after. He was ashamed before his father, who told him he had his Maker's perception. The son then studied twelve years; by his return his wife was infertile. Rabbi said divorce or a second wife would both shame her. Her husband prayed for her, and she was cured.
10.why: The Gemara is discussing how often Torah scholars owe their wives marital relations, through a run of stories about scholars away at study. This one weighs years of study against a wife's needs, and the price she pays.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Yehuda HaNasi; he arranges two matches for his son and worries over the son's infertile wife.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: His family was the first match for Rabbi's son; the girl died.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
people.about: His daughter became the wife of Rabbi's son; his family agreed to support twelve years of study.

terms.meaning: The document, called a ketubba, written at a Jewish wedding, recording the husband's obligations to his wife.
Rabbi tells his son he acted as God did: according to the two verses, God first planned the Sanctuary for after the people entered the Land, then moved it earlier out of love.

11.note: At the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai set off for the study hall. Rabbi Shimon asked him to wait so they could go together, but he did not wait. He studied for twelve years, and when he came back the streets of his city had changed and he could not find his house. Sitting by the river, he heard people calling to a girl: Daughter of Hakhinai, fill your pitcher and come. Realizing she was his own daughter, he followed her home. His wife, sifting flour, looked up and saw him; her heart fluttered and she died. He said: Master of the universe, is this the reward of this poor woman? He prayed for her, and she lived.
11.why: This is one of a string of stories about scholars who leave their wives for years of study, told while the Gemara discusses how often scholars owe their wives marital relations.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai
people.about: Leaves for twelve years of study and comes home a stranger to his own town.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: Newly married; asks Rabbi Hananya to wait so they can go to the study hall together.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students gathered to learn Torah, often far from home.

12.note: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa spent twelve years in the study hall. When he came back he decided not to walk in on his family suddenly, so he sat in the local study hall and sent word home. His son Rabbi Oshaya, whom he did not recognize, came and sat before him and asked him questions of law. Seeing how sharp the young man was, Rabbi Hama was distressed and said: Had I been here, I would have had a child like this. He went home, the son came in too, and Rabbi Hama stood up for him, thinking he had come with another question. His wife said: Is there a father who stands up before his son? Rami bar Hama applied to Rabbi Oshaya the verse 'A threefold cord is not quickly broken.'
12.why: Rabbi Hama explicitly avoids what ben Hakhinai did in the story just before, whose sudden return stopped his wife's heart. It belongs to the Gemara's run of stories about scholars away from home for years.

people.name: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa
people.about: Returns from twelve years of study and does not recognize his own son.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: Rabbi Hama's son, already a sharp scholar when his father returns.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: Applies the verse about a threefold cord to Rabbi Oshaya.

terms.term: A threefold cord is not quickly broken
terms.meaning: A verse from Ecclesiastes 4:12, applied to Rabbi Oshaya as the third generation of scholars in his family.

13.note: Rabbi Akiva was a shepherd for the rich ben Kalba Savua. His daughter saw his modesty and asked: If I betroth myself to you, will you go to study? He said yes. Her father heard, threw her out and vowed she would get nothing of his property. Akiva studied twelve years and came back with twelve thousand students. He overheard an old man ask her how long she would live as a living man's widow; she said that if he listened to her, he would study twelve more. Taking that as permission, he left again and returned with twenty-four thousand. She went out in her poor clothes, fell at his feet and kissed them. When his attendants pushed her away he said: Leave her; mine and yours is hers. Her father came to have his vow undone, learned who Akiva was, kissed his feet and gave him half his money.
13.why: It closes the Gemara's run of stories about scholars who spend twelve years away studying. In the others the wife pays for the absence; here she sends him and asks for more.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A shepherd who becomes a great scholar after twenty-four years of study, sent by his wife.

people.name: ben Kalba Savua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's wealthy employer, who throws out his daughter for marrying Akiva and later seeks him out.

people.name: ben Azzai
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's daughter did for him what her mother had done for Akiva.

terms.meaning: A binding oath; here the father swore his daughter could have no benefit from his property. A Sage can sometimes undo a vow made on a mistaken assumption.
A woman who lives alone for years while her husband is still alive but away.
To enter the first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage.

14.note: Rava sent his son, Rav Yosef, to study with the Sage Rav Yosef, and they set the term at six years. After three years, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the son said he would go and see his family. His father heard, took up a weapon and went out to meet him. He said: Did you remember your mistress? Some say he said: Did you remember your dove? The two were so caught up that neither of them ate the last meal before the fast.
14.why: It ends the Gemara's string of stories about students who leave home for years to study, part of its discussion of what a scholar owes his wife. Here it is the father who will not let the son break off his studies.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: Sent to study for six years; wants to visit home after three.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Yosef's father, who goes out armed to stop his son coming home.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage the son was sent to study with.

terms.meaning: The last meal eaten on the eve of Yom Kippur before the fast begins.
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year, observed with a full day's fast.

15.note: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband and was holding on to a garment. Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat with Rav Gamda and said that a wife who rebels loses her worn clothes. Rav Gamda said: Because Rav Zevid is a great man you flatter him? Didn't Rav Kahana say that Rava raised this question and did not resolve it? In another version, the three said she does not lose her worn clothes, and Rav Gamda said: Because Rav Zevid is a great man, you twist the judgment against him? Rava left it unresolved.
15.why: The Gemara is setting out the law of a 'rebellious' wife. Since the question was never settled, it concludes from this episode that what she has already seized is not taken from her, and what she has not seized is not given to her.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: His daughter-in-law is the rebellious wife; the Sages are accused of bending the law because of his greatness.

people.name: Rav Gamda
people.about: Rebukes the three Sages for ruling on a question Rava left open.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: One of the three Sages who rule on the case.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: One of the three Sages who rule on the case.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: One of the three Sages who rule on the case.

terms.meaning: In this discussion, a wife who refuses her husband marital relations (or, in one view, her household duties); the court reduces what her marriage contract will pay her.
Clothing a bride brought into the marriage as part of her dowry, which may since have become worn but still exists.

16.note: After Abaye died, his widow Homa came before Rava, the judge, and asked him to set her support. He did. She asked for wine as well. Rava said he knew Nahmani (Abaye) did not drink wine. She swore by his life that Abaye gave her wine in cups this big, and as she showed him, her arm was uncovered and a light shone in the courtroom. Rava went home and asked his wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, for relations. She asked who had been in court today. He said: Homa, Abaye's wife. She went after Homa and beat her with the lock of a chest until she drove her out of all of Mehoza, saying: You have killed three, and now you come to kill another?
16.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a widow's support includes wine. Rava assumes it depends on whether she drank in her husband's lifetime; the case after it gives wine by local custom in Mehoza.

people.name: Homa
people.about: Abaye's widow; Rava's wife accuses her of having killed three (the translation explains: three husbands).

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who sets Homa's support.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Homa's late husband, also called Nahmani.

people.name: daughter of Rav Hisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who drives Homa out of the city.

terms.meaning: A widow is entitled to food and upkeep from her late husband's estate; the court sets the amount.
A polite oath addressed to the Sage, like saying 'I swear to you'.

17.note: Riding out of Jerusalem with his students, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman picking barley out of Arabs' animals' dung. Covering herself with her hair, she asked him for support; she was the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon. Asked where her father's money had gone, she quoted a Jerusalem proverb that money lacks salt, or by another reading that kindness is its salt; her father-in-law's wealth, she said, was lost along with it. She reminded him he had signed her marriage contract; he told his students it listed a million gold dinars from her father alone. He wept: when Israel does God's will no nation rules them, and when they do not, they are handed even to a lowly nation's animals. Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swears he saw her gathering barley among horses' hooves in Akko.
17.why: The Gemara has just told how the Sages granted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter four hundred gold coins for perfume from her late husband's estate; this tells what later became of her.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Meets the ruined woman on the road and remembers signing her marriage contract.

people.name: the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: Once immensely rich, now gathering barley from animal dung.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: Her father, a man of vast wealth whose charity the Gemara questions.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Swears he saw her gathering barley among horses' hooves in Akko.

terms.meaning: The document, called a ketubba, written at a wedding; it records what the bride brings and what the husband owes her.
A name for God, meaning the One who is everywhere.

terms.term: According to the camel is the burden
terms.meaning: A proverb: the stronger the camel, the heavier its load. The Gemara uses it to say Nakdimon gave less charity than a man of his wealth should have.

18.note: Hillel the Elder provided a poor man from a good family with a horse to ride and a servant to run in front of him. One time Hillel could not find a servant to run before him, so Hillel himself ran in front of him for three mil.
18.why: The Sages read the verse 'sufficient for his deficiency in that which is deficient for him' as requiring charity to supply what a poor person lacks, even a horse and a servant for one who was used to them; Hillel's deed is told as an example.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: Provides a once-wealthy poor man with a horse and a servant, and once runs before him himself.

terms.meaning: A measure of distance, roughly a kilometer or a little over half a mile.

19.note: A man came to Rabbi Nehemya asking for charity. Rabbi Nehemya asked what he usually ate, and he said fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya asked whether he would be willing to share his own meal of lentils. The man ate lentils with him, and he died. Rabbi Nehemya said: Woe to this one who was killed by Nehemya.
19.why: After cases of charity giving a once-wealthy poor man what he was used to, this one shows the other side. The Gemara asks why Rabbi Nehemya did not say 'woe to Nehemya', and explains he meant the man was to blame for pampering himself so.

people.name: Rabbi Nehemya
people.about: Offers a poor man used to rich food a share of his own lentils.

20.note: A man came to Rava asking for charity. Rava asked what he usually ate, and he said fattened hen and aged wine. Rava asked whether he was not worried about burdening the community. The man answered: Do I eat from what is theirs? I eat from what the Merciful One gives, citing a verse that God gives each person his food in his own time. Just then Rava's sister, who had not seen him for thirteen years, arrived and brought him a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava said: What is this before me? and told the man: I have answered you; get up and eat.
20.why: The Gemara is discussing how far charity must go to meet a poor person's accustomed standard. Coming after the man who died eating Rabbi Nehemya's lentils, this story supports giving such a man what he is used to.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Questions a poor man's expensive tastes, then gives way when the same foods arrive at his door.

people.name: Rava's sister
people.about: Arrives after thirteen years away bringing exactly the food the man asked for.

terms.meaning: A name for God.
